# Copper November 2010 

- All in all, it was a long and hectic ride during a month in which, ultimately, prices have ended up largely where they began.  That said, we believe that the market has managed to hold ground despite some potentially damaging fundamentals emerging during the month, and we put this down to a widespread view that, going forward, supply concerns will continue to shape the market (and prices). 

- In fact, we are already anticipating a market deficit of close to 300kt for the final quarter of this year, and this is likely to increase to 0.56Mt on an annual basis in 2011.  This is based on the conservative assumption of 7% copper demand growth from China, and 4.8% globally. 

- During October, trader concentrates spot buying and selling terms increased pretty much in tandem, however, in November there has been a disparity between movements in these rates with selling terms (traders to smelters) continuing to rise, by around $8/t & 0.8c/lb, but with buying terms having stabilised in the range $75/t & 7.5c/lb to $82/t & 8.2c/lb, with prompt shipments typically attracting numbers at the higher end of this range.  This disparity appears to have been caused by a change in the cash-to-3s price spread with October having traded predominantly in contango compared with a widening back during November. 

- A key attribute of the concentrates market is that spot terms can influence sentiment during the annual Mating Season negotiations.  From the perspective of the sellers, 2011 is shaping up to be very similar to this year in the sense that concentrate availability are likely to satisfy +/- 80% of primary smelter capacity once again.  For this reason the major concentrate producers are looking for a roll over of long-term RC/RCs, i.e. $46.5/t & 4.65c/lb. However, the very large increase in spot TC/RCs during the latter stages of 2010 has encouraged many custom smelters to raise their 2011 long-term TC/RC expectations to between $75-80/t & 7.5-8.0c/lb.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**Copper begins the month on a lower note…** Having given a brief nod to the targeted US$8500/t mark ($3.86/lb) on October 25<sup>th</sup> , we ex

pected copper prices to fall back in the very near term, and this indeed was the case.  For the following eight trading days, through to November 4<sup>th</sup> , copper remained largely well below US$8400/t, dipping to a low of US$8225/t ($3.73/lb - cash), as all metals awaited the announcement about quantitative easing (QE) from the US Federal Reserve.  When this came in, most metals resumed their former upward track – not because the QE II effort held any surprises either way (indeed, it looked like the market was happy to see it out of the way because it maintained the generally declining direction of the dollar), but because it meant that metals could return to news and events pertaining to their own particular fundamentals.  And in copper, all eyes had been looking towards Chile, where the possibility of a strike at the world’s fourth largest mine was growing stronger by the day. 

**..but industrial action in Chile brings supply concerns back to the fore…** Rumours of potential industrial action by the 1550 workers at Xstrata/Anglo American’s Collahuasi mine had already made old news of the QE II announcement on the 4<sup>th</sup> , and cash prices kicked up a notch to US$8521/t ($3.87/lb) as a result.  But the tradition of setting off fireworks in the UK on the evening of November 5<sup>th</sup> was brought forward into the daylight hours as the official announcement of a strike at Collahuasi lit up LME prices by over $175/t on that day, to US$8698/t ($3.95/lb).  But even then the metal was not done.  Pausing on the 8<sup>th</sup> to acknowledge that the miners would continue bargaining, cash prices again surged on the 9<sup>th</sup> by another $172/t once it became clear that an early resolution was not going to be found.  Copper closed out that day at US$8844/t ($4.01/lb) as price makers digested the effect of losing up to 10kt copper contained in concentrates for each week of downtime in what has become a tight market already. 

**..and pushes cash prices to a 28-month high** A statement on the 9<sup>th</sup> /10<sup>th</sup> November by company officials that concentrate production and shipments had not been disrupted – and were unlikely to be for some time – did little to calm the markets and restrain price strength.  By the 11<sup>th</sup> , LME cash surged again to US$8925/t ($4.05/lb) – the highest closing price since July 3<sup>rd</sup> , 2008 - and the cash to three-month spread remained in a backwardation for the third straight day. 

**Bearish industry data from China – and economic news from Eire - turn the tide again** However, prices headed south for the following three days as attention turned to bearish headlines coming out of China.  On the 12<sup>th</sup> , news of lower output of refined copper during October, combined with another hefty weekly increase (+8.6kt) in Shanghai stocks (to 115.4kt) lent further support to prior concerns that copper demand had fallen away quite dramatically during that month.  The driving fo

rce for lower metals prices across the board, including copper, came after speculation that China would increase interest rates in order to curb inflation. Copper prices “lost” $212/t that day, but more was to come over that weekend with the increasing noise regarding European country debt levels. Both regional concerns brought the emphasis back to the exchange rate story to which we had grown accustomed over the last few months, and the immediate prospects of a stronger dollar pinned copper prices back to US$8145/t ($3.69/lb) by the 17th . #### **Copper price and $US trade-weighted index** 9500

**But the exchange rate story fails this time to make a long-lasting impact** Cash copper picked up $240/t on the 18th with market makers being of the opinion that the sell-off had been overdone, and once it became clear by the 19th that China would not increase interest rates after all, the exchange rate prop fell away and cash surged again to $8400/t (US$3.81/lb). Equally, the markets felt somewhat relieved that Eire took the €85Bn bail-out money after initially denying it was even in talks to do so, and were then comforted by the belief that no other country was next in line – at least, for this month. **Chinese trade data keep the lid on a late-month rally** But that price level could not withstand the apparent bearishness of China’s October trade statistics, released on the 22nd and 23rd , which had many price-makers again questioning underlying levels of demand there. The near 30% decline in refined copper imports over September’s figure dovetailed well into prior commentary that demand had fallen away since the start of Q3, and the immediate reaction was seen in a near $260/t fall in closing cash prices once again, to below US$8150/t (US$3.69/lb). Subsequent calm under more rational analysis (see Consumption section) allowed prices to recover somewhat, but US$8300/t ($3.75/lb) seemed to be the level at which copper would see out the month. #### **Shanghai/LME arbitrage ($/t) vs refined copper imports** 600 Refin

**Market holds ground in face of short-term Chinese bearishness** All in all, it seemed a long and hectic ride during a month in which, ultimately, prices have ended up largely where they began. That said, we believe that the market has managed to hold ground despite some potentially damaging fundamentals emerging during the month, and we put this down to a widespread view that, going forward, supply concerns will continue to shape the market (and prices). Additionally, we believe that the more bearish aspects to the market this month have a short-term nature about them that should relatively easily be usurped by medium-term, structurally price-supportive, issues. For example, that Shanghai copper stocks rose most of the month to a recent high of 126.7kt by the 19th was indeed a factor behind prices and premia softening at that time. But, as with the other unfavourable data to emerge from China during the month, a lot of it was due to the fact that the Golden Week holidays took six working days out of the month; a week later, stocks had declined by 4kt to 122.6kt on the 26th and arguably pointed to a nation returning to “business as usual”. Offsetting the SHFE increase, stocks on the LME fell by a further 10kt during the month, to 357kt on the 26th , and Comex stocks dropped 2.3kt to 65.8kt. A greater cause for concern than rising SHFE stocks, though, came with the discussion - albeit brief - over the (unknown) quantity of stocks held in bonded warehouses in China. Initial reports that they had “doubled” since July could easily have pushed copper below the US$8000/t resistance level that now appears to be in place. But again, a calmer view prevailed once it was accepted that the material (and the opinions on tonnages range from 200-600kt) will stay in bond unless financing it becomes a problem, or when domestic prices become sufficiently strong (and significantly above the LME) to justify such a move. Although the arbitrage between the LME and SHFE has narrowed this month, the differential has not yet been overturned to encourage the switch out of bonded warehouses. **Reasonable demand growth will support prices…** But we believe that as the market comes to appreciate the growing tightne

ss from the supply side going forward, the shorter-term issues will take a back seat.  We are already anticipating a market deficit of close to 300kt for the final quarter of this year, and this is likely to increase to 0.56Mt on an annual basis in 2011.  This is based on the conservative assumption of 7% copper demand growth from China, and 4.8% globally. That Codelco set its Grade A spot copper premium to China at $115/t (up by 35% on this year, and significantly higher than the $98/t fixed for Europe and South Korea) says a good deal about its expectations of demand there for 2011. 

**..as will medium-term supply issues** In response to the demand growth, however, we can see production improving by only 3.1% in 2011.  Even this may well be tested.  Workers at Antofagasta’s Los Pelambres and at Codelco’s Radomiro Tomic may well have agreed a new contract in the final full week of November, but those at Collahuasi remain out.  Also, late this month, Rio’s subsidiary, Kennecott Utah Copper Co (KUCC), stated that copper contained in mine production will be 10% lower in 2011 due to weaker ore tenors.  This is something that has been seen already over the past four quarters – ore grades dipping from 0.6% Cu in Q3 2009 to 0.48% in Q2 2010 and to 0.55% in Q3 – while average concentrate grades have also fallen from >29% Cu to ~25% Cu.  KUCC could counter some of that mine feed loss by buying in (or tolling) concentrates, but it has not bought third-party feed in significant quantities for some years, and may not consider that it is financially justifiable to do so. 

**But it is not just market prices that should move up as a result of such operational difficulties** Such issues as these at KUCC are likely to keep premia in North America higher rather than lower going forward.  Equally, the fact that we have lost two North American refineries this year (Kidd Creek’s 120kt/a in May and White Pine’s 60kt/a in July), plus potential anode tightness at CCR in Montreal through 2011, should all conspire to push premia up.  Already, we hear that one leading cathode supplier is testing the market for an additional 1.5c/lb in premia quotations for 2011.

Meanwhile, in Europe, we now know that the Russian government has re-imposed the 10% duty on refined copper cathode exports and this should come into force by mid-December.  Last time this occurred, we saw a significant reduction in cathode exports from Russia to Europe as producers converted the cathode into rod at home to dodge the tax.  Consequently, Europe can expect to see some tightness in cathode supplies going into 2011, and premia could easily edge up as a result.  The one significant difference this time around though is that this past summer Uralelectromed’s Pyshma refinery obtained “good delivery” status from the LME, having pursued a multi-year strategic plan to upgrade its equipment and standardise the

quality of its material. This might allow Pyshma to obtain better prices in the export market than before and reduce the impact of the new tax. **Price forecasts to average $4/lb for the next two years** Under these circumstances, any analysis of such traditional fundamentals alone would suggest a price risk profile leaning towards the upside going forward. But add in the spectre of two or more exchange traded funds acquiring and holding physical metal and that profile is further enhanced. As we said last month, given that one of the key criteria for a physical metal ETF to succeed is higher short- to medium-term prices (backed either by a real or perceived market shortage), then our current price outlook of four-dollar average copper for the next two years versus the $2.34/lb in 2009 and likely $3.38/lb for this year does not look so aggressive. #### **Price forecasts and world quarterly supply/demand balance – (kt)** |||**Refined**

Further out, our 2012 forecast shows equally robust growth of 4.1%, and continues the long-standing trend of the decline in demand in mature economies being offset by significant growth in developing economies. ### **Europe and CIS** **Regional copper demand estimate for 2010 holds firm at 3.96Mt** We have made only one minor change to our demand data for Europe this month, and this has come from Belgium, where anecdotal evidence and trade data are implying slightly hi

gher demand than we had been showing. Consequently, we have added a further 22kt of copper consumption to this year’s estimate, which now stands at 272kt. In Italy, copper and alloy semis production figures for the third quarter from the national non-ferrous metals association, Assomet, largely held to expectations in that overall output was lower q-o-q at 244kt _vs._ 301kt for the prior three-month period, but 18% up on the same period in 2009. As a result, we have left our 2010 copper demand estimate for Italy unchanged at 592kt. **Eire becomes the second country to take a bail out after Greece** The past month has shown that the region’s debt crisis is far from over, and its financial sector far from secure. While the crisis has few implications for metals demand in the short term, over the longer run it reinforces the expected underperformance of European economies, especially those who will struggle to meet debt obligations and are unable to boost competitiveness by devaluation or inflate away their debt while a member of the single currency. Prolonged fiscal consolidation will depress growth for a number of years, and our declining copper demand profile reflects that general reality. There is little chance of further QE from the ECB providing a boost, as its balance sheet is already stretched, and the idea of potentially higher inflation will not sit well with Germany in particular. **Regional industrial production growth slowed to 0.8% q-o-q in Q3, from 2.3% in the previous two quarters** The slowdown was expected, given the end to fiscal boosts and inventory adjustments. September in particular was an average month only, with activity contracting in both Germany and the euro zone as a whole. Nevertheless, the region’s economic performance has exceeded the expectations of many, and still shows solid signs of growth in the coming months. Both the output and new orders components of the EU PMI climbed in October, to 55.16 and 54.96 respectively. In Germany, the IFO index showed that sentiment in both current manufacturing conditions and future outlook have improved. The headline IFO index hit its highest level since May 2007. European flash PMI data have yet again defied the odds, rising to 55.5 in November from 54.6 in the previous month. This is the second consecutive month of gains to strong levels, suggesting manufacturing activity in Europe is very robust. #### **Italian production of copper semis** 40 320

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - November 2010 Page 6 of 23 Copper Monthly Update **Autos sector suffers in October…** That said, in autos, car sales in Western Europe in October were down by 18% y-oy at just under 1M units, and well below the 2010 average

of 1.1M.  Given that the overwhelming majority of European cars produced do not leave Europe, prospects for further gains in production are weak.  In October, Germany produced 536k vehicles, up by just 1% y-o-y and down 6% from September.  This underlines the feast-to-famine nature of the auto business, and manufacturers of wire for auto-related harnesses (many of which having been relocated to Eastern Europe) are complaining of that particular business having fallen away entirely. 

**..while construction resumes its earlier downward path** Meanwhile in the construction sector, September’s bullish PMI numbers turned out to be a bit of a false dawn, as all three datasets relating to housing, commercial and civil contracted in October.  This has not entirely fed through to copper use in the albeit small UK market, at least, where public expenditure on buildings (such as hospitals and police stations) and certain infrastructure (e.g. train track and energy-related requirements) has sustained copper wire use, according to one of our contacts.  This portion of spending will probably dry up with the public expenditure cuts coming through with the new fiscal year from next April, though, but again any drop here may be offset by the preparations for the 2012 Olympic Games, which are already coming into view. From our conversations, we understand that many of the larger wire and cable suppliers are reasonably busy attending to bids for this large-scale business, and leaving their regular, run-of-the-mill business to smaller players. 

Already there is a consensus building that this shift in supplier structure will allow higher prices to be obtained on the “non-Olympics” business into 2011.  For now, though, we are also learning that wire and cable wholesalers in the UK have stopped buying as we near the year’s end for inventory control purposes.  Some of their suppliers, however, believe this decision has come a little too early, and will leave the wholesalers short of material as we enter the New Year.  If this also applies to other areas of Europe, there could be a rush for new orders in January. 

**M&A activity over Draka raises a lot of interest** A lot of the chatter this month in Europe, though, has taken place at the merger and acquisitions level, as Amsterdam-based Draka Holdings put itself up for sale.  Being the third-largest producer within Europe of low-voltage and special-purpose cable and having a global wire and cable presence, Draka has naturally attracted the interest of Prysmian Cables and Systems of Italy and Nexans of France.  But as they vied to outbid each other in the race to control Draka, the most recent bid has come from Tianjin, China-based Xinmao, which has put a €1Bn bid on the table.  As this is 20% higher than the last offer from Prysmian, Draka Holdings is giving it due attention, and we await to see if there will be any counter bid from the Europeans. 

**B3 Eire equipment sold to Russian companies** Across the seas in E

ire, we note that much of the equipment that was in place at the B3 Cables Solutions Longford plant went under the hammer this month, and was largely sold to Russian wire and cable producers.  B3, which made cables for the telecoms market and was one of only two cable-makers left in Eire, was owned by both ABB and BICC in the past, actually folded in July following an 80% collapse in its order books. Its most significant customer, we believe, was the national telecoms provider Eircom, which was privatised in May 2006 and sold to Australian investment group, Babcock and Brown. 

### **Americas** 

**US provides encouraging macro data during October** Industrial production in October was virtually unchanged from the previous quarter, despite the strength of vehicle production.  The main plus point in the data was capital goods output (up by 1.1% on the month) making eight straight months of growth and showing that business spending continues to improve.  Lead indicators remain encouraging despite the lack of momentum in industrial production growth.  The PMI accelerated to 56.9 in October from 54.4 in September, while new orders hit a 5-month high of 58.9.  The apparent disconnect between IP and the PMI is worrying, but at least the PMIs suggest that IP is not likely to contract any time in the next 6 months. 

Retail sales increased by 1.2% mom in October – the 4<sup>th</sup> straight month of expansion, and are up by 7.3% y-o-y.  While not much related to metal demand directly, the data improvement is important, in that a sustainable and vigorous recovery in the US will eventually be kick-started by consumer spending.  October was a very encouraging month for the US auto industry.  Total vehicle production accelerated to an annualised rate of 8.2m units (up 15.3% y-o-y) – the second strongest month since mid 2008.  The driver of growth was the light trucks market, which has defied expectations by significantly outperforming cars in 2010.  The strength in production is mirrored in sales, which expanded by 13.4% y-o-y in October.  The details of the data were a positive in that retail sales were strong and incentive schemes relatively few. This suggests that sustained improvements in the underlying rate of consumer demand in the vehicle market may be in the offing. 

**Copper rod output remains strong…** Meanwhile, production of copper wire rod for August of c.110kt (and a revised July figure of 112.6kt) have maintained the average output rate at some 10% higher than the first eight months of last year.  Despite the poor construction sector, strong performances from autos, which are on target for a c.15% year on year increase in output, will have contributed to the robust rod output.  Even so, as we noted last month, shipments remained slightly below ongoing production rates through to August at 109.5kt, and so rod inventory climbed to 24.1kt at the end of that month, from July’s 23.8kt, according to data from the American Bureau of Metal Statistic

**..but tube sector continues to suffer due to poor construction rates** If the US wire rod sector seems to be holding up reasonably well this year, the same cannot be said for the tube business, reflecting the poor construction market. Negative equity from housing fallout will continue to be the main drag. According to latest American Bureau of Metal Statistics data, apparent consumption of copper tube remained 10% down to August this year vs. the same period in 2009 at 222kt. Equally, domestic shipments remained depressed, down by 8% at 184kt, and this low level of business has continued to pose problems for even some of the bigger players. On November 1st , Huntsville, Alabama-based Wolverine Tube Inc filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings in order to restructure its $100M of debt. Given that it has the support of its noteholders, Wolverine hopes to emerge from bankruptcy within 90 days with c.$30M of debt but at more favourable repayment terms and to continue operating in the interim. Wolverine’s move comes almost a year after another player in the fragmented tube business – Cambridge-Lee Industries, and its Mexican parent Cobre de Pasteje – both filed for Chapter 11 proceedings in December 2009. #### **US brass mill shipments – (kt)** 20 100

Wolverine - a manufacturer of copper and alloy tube, fabricated products and metal joining products - has been a lossmaking entity for the past three years at least, and so the move into Chapter 11 will come as no surprise. The company closed and sold three manufacturing plants in the US and Canada between 2006-2008, and reduced its holding in a Shanghai plant in two stages during 2008 to 50%. For the last 2009 reported period on record (January 1st -October 4th , 2009), WTI shipped around 43kt of products, down by roughly 28% on the Jan-Sept period in 2008. Cathode and scrap requirements for its heavily reduced North American facilities amounted to c.20kt in that 2009 period, down from c.47kt Metals Market Service Monthly Update - November 2010 Page 8 of 23 Copper Monthly Update for the whole of 2008. For the period Jan 1st to April 4th 2010, WTI shipped 7.1kt of finished products, down 12.5% from the same period in 2009 due to the poor

construction market. 

Meanwhile, Mueller Industries reported that production levels at its copper and alloy tube-making facilities in North America, the UK and China are still operating at significantly less than capacity, despite some improvement to September this year over 2009.  US residential and commercial construction levels – which are the backbone to the tube business – remains affected by the general economic downturn.   The headline 8% improvement in housing starts to September 2010 vs. the first nine months of 2009 appears good but comes off a low base; equally, the August 2010 seasonally-adjusted annualized rate of non-residential value of construction “put in place” figure of almost $260Bn was 24% down on the equivalent measure for August 2009.  In both areas, though, Mueller believes the low points are passed, and that 2011 will bring an upturn in business. 

### **China** 

**Mostly bullish macro economic sentiment and data from China…** China’s CPI surged 4.4% year-on-year in October, a 25-month high.  From January to October, China's CPI rose 3% y-o-y, hitting the government's target ceiling for the year.  As the government has been striving to cool inflation, its central bank ordered all banks to set aside more reserves this month in an effort to rein in liquidity, and this brought some concern in metals markets that demand would be effectively curtailed until the New Year. 

Fixed asset investment continued on its steady clip, growing by 23.7% y-o-y in October.  Year to date, FAI has grown by 24.4% in nominal terms and 20.2% in real terms.  Real estate investment has been the star performer in FAI this year, increasing by 36.5% y-o-y, but given the tighter conditions, it is hard to make a case for such growth to continue into 2011.  Investment in the real estate sector increased by 37% in October. 

China's industrial value-added output increased by 13.1% y-o-y in October from 13.3% in September.  The growth rate for the first 10 months was 16.1% y-o-y, down 0.2% from the January-September period.  The PMI continued to accelerate in October, suggesting solid momentum behind Chinese growth in Q1 of next year.  With real interest rates negative, big ticket purchases are encouraged and this should provide a further boost to consumer durables production.

**Chinese concentrate imports fall by 31% month on month in October** After importing a record tonnage (683.5kdmt) of concentrates in September, shipments to China fell by 31% month on month in October but this was still almost 4% higher on a year-on-year basis.  Cumulative imports during the first ten months now stand at 5.4Mdmt which is an uplift of 5.9% in comparison with the same period in 2009.  For the year as a whole and barring any abnormal variations in receipts during November and December, China is expected to import between 6.3Mdmt and 6.4Mdmt which would represent an increase of between 2% and 4% over last year’s total. 

**China becoming more successful in influencing spot market terms** The meteoric rise in China’s appetite for copper has been such that the country now consumes almost 7.4Mt/a of copper cathodes, but is only able to satisfy 1.7Mt/a of this in the form of primary and secondary domestic supplies.  The majority of the country’s copper requirements are thus met by imports that currently comprise 2.9Mt/a of refined copper, 0.8Mt/a of scrap, 0.4Mt/a of blister and 1.6Mt/a of copper-in-concentrates.  Ten years ago Japan was the largest importer of internationally traded copper concentrates with a market share of 33%, with China in second place with 13%.  By 2008 China had nudged marginally ahead with 26% compared with Japan’s 25%.  This year we estimate that China’s market share will rise to 29% and potentially to in excess of 35% by 2013.  Despite its growing market dominance the general perception has been that China has not been particular

ly successful in exerting a coordinated influence in the spot market as regards the timing of its purchases, especially in the lead up to the annual concentrate Mating Season. Indeed the overriding trend over the past few years has been for the CSPT to be reasonably successful in coordinating a floor on spot rates in a rising TC/RC market only to end up in a “free for all” amongst smelters when spot terms were falling. While this has certainly been the perception, an analysis of Chinese spot terms over time actually paints a different picture. The following analysis has been derived from monthly spot TC/RC data over the period 2001 to 2010. We have identified minimum/maximum monthly spot TC/RCs for each of these years and have then expressed each month’s spot rates as a percentage of the annual range in minimum/maximum terms. In this manner we have “normalised” charges for each year with the lowest monthly spot TC/RC being 0% and the highest being 100%. We have then averaged these percentages for each month over the past ten years categorising them into three distinct time periods. The chart below shows these average monthly variations for these periods, i.e. 2001-2004, 2005-2007 and 2008-2010 and a clear pattern is quite evident. During the period 20012004 the general trend in spot rates was for a decline throughout the year. Between 2005 and 2007 a similar decline can be seen through to September after which terms spike up coincident with the annual Mating Season. More latterly, over the period 2008 to 2010 Chinese spot terms have been at their lowest between April and August and have then risen very markedly through the key Mating Season months of September through November. This implies that Chinese smelting industry is potentially becoming more sophisticated as regards its buying patterns and the influence of these on spot TC/RCs in relation to the annual Mating Season. That said part of the year-end rise in spot rates is also due to a surge in spot concentrates availability with miners seeking to minimise their year-end inventories. #### **Variations in Monthly Chinese Spot TC/RCs as % of Annual Range: 2001 - 2010** 100%
